title: Inside the Fake Celebrity Podcast Scam Fooling Hollywood

reading.body:
This incident shows an impersonation attack at scale, where scammers used AI to generate personalized emails impersonating Terry Gross and other "Fresh Air" staff to target authors and public figures. The emails included specific details about recipients' work and requested payment for supposed production costs. The fraud operated at the point of initial contact, before any human verification could occur.

The deployment failure was organizational: WHYY, NPR and "Fresh Air" had no mechanism to stop fraudulent emails sent in their names from reaching targets, and no way to prevent scammers from claiming authority they did not have. Catching this would have required either recipients verifying invitations through official channels before engaging, or the organizations publicly warning their audience that they never charge guests and providing verification methods.

It is not established whether the AI systems used were specifically built or trained for this purpose, or whether they were general tools repurposed by scammers.

reports.title: ‘Too good to be true?’: No, WHYY’s Terry Gross did not personally email you to be a guest on ‘Fresh Air’
Inside the Fake Celebrity Podcast Scam Fooling Hollywood

summary:
Scammers are sending personalized emails impersonating Terry Gross and other "Fresh Air" staff members to lure authors, entertainers and public figures into a fraudulent scheme. The messages include detailed references to the targets' work and appear to come from legitimate production staff. After recipients express interest, they receive follow-up emails requesting payment of fees like $250 for supposed production costs. Misericordia University professor Jennifer Black initially thought she had genuinely been invited to discuss her book but became suspicious when the email came directly from Gross herself and mentioned payment.

According to cybersecurity experts, artificial intelligence has made these social engineering scams more sophisticated and personalized than previous fraud attempts. WHYY, NPR and "Fresh Air" have confirmed the fraudulent emails and are investigating with law enforcement. The organization emphasized it never charges guests for interviews. Red flags include requests for money, personal email addresses instead of official ones, and the implausibility of major show hosts personally handling logistics. Experts advise recipients to verify invitations through official channels rather than responding to suspicious messages.
